820.title: The ladder of love
820.hook: Diotima teaches Socrates that love climbs from one beautiful person to beauty itself (Symposium 210–211)
820.howItsDone: Readers of Plato's Symposium, in philosophy classes and in some mystical writing shaped by Plato, discuss Diotima's ascent from the love of one person to the love of beauty itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many words for love. Your line was many words. Did you catch which kind you meant? Today, one more Greek word, and a staircase. Day eight hundred twenty.

A dinner party in Athens, in Plato's Symposium. The guests agree to go easy on the wine and take turns giving speeches in praise of love. When it's Socrates' turn, he does something odd for a famous talker. He doesn't offer his own view. He says a woman taught him what love is, a wise woman from Mantinea named Diotima, and he simply passes on her lesson. What she taught him has a shape, and the shape is a climb.
screen: `A DINNER PARTY IN ATHENS.` → `SOCRATES PASSES IT ON.` → `DIOTIMA OF MANTINEA.`

segments.voice: First, one beautiful person. The Greek word all night is eros, love as longing, love that wants what it doesn't yet have. Diotima says this love often begins with one beautiful person, and the lover is moved to speak beautiful words. Second, beauty in others. Then the lover notices that the beauty in one body is akin to the beauty in another, and the love widens past a single face. Third, beauty of soul. Next comes the beauty of minds and character, then the beauty in good laws and ways of living, then the beauty of knowledge. Fourth, beauty itself. At the top, Diotima says, the lover suddenly sees a beauty that doesn't grow or fade, isn't lovely in one way and ugly in another, and is the source of every beautiful thing below it. Readers call it the ladder of love, because she describes going up as if by steps. It's easy to hear this as climbing away from people, and some readers do hear it that way. Others hear it differently: the first love isn't thrown away, it's the bottom rung, and without it there's no ladder at all. Plato leaves room for both readings. What's plain in the text is the direction. Love, for Diotima, is a reaching, and it keeps reaching past the thing it started with.
screen: `ONE BEAUTIFUL PERSON.` · `BEAUTY IN OTHERS.` · `BEAUTY OF SOUL.` · `BEAUTY ITSELF.` · then, large: `THE LADDER OF LOVE.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on something beautiful near you, or bring one to mind: a face, a line of music, a kind act you once saw, an idea that made you sit up. Stay with it for a few breaths. Then let your attention climb one step. What is it in this that lifts you? Not the thing itself, but its beauty. Notice where that takes you, without forcing it any higher. If nothing comes, stay on the first rung; it's part of the ladder too. The bell holds the time.
The ladder of love. Diotima's lesson in Plato's Symposium: love that climbs, step by step, from one beautiful person toward beauty itself. Today's word.
Your line: the ladder. Today, when something beautiful stops you, ask what it might be a step toward. Day eight hundred twenty.

821.title: The other half
821.hook: Aristophanes' myth: humans split in two, searching for their other half (Symposium 189–193)
821.howItsDone: Aristophanes' myth from Plato's Symposium is read in philosophy and literature classes, and its picture of searching for one's other half turns up in writing about love; readers take it as comedy, as a myth, or both.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diotima's staircase. Your line was the ladder. Did something beautiful lift you a step? Today, the same dinner party, and a very different speech. Day eight hundred twenty-one.

Earlier that night at the Symposium, before Socrates speaks, it's the comic playwright Aristophanes' turn, and he has the hiccups. A doctor at the table tells him to hold his breath, then to gargle with water, and if all else fails, to tickle his nose and sneeze. The doctor speaks in his place while he recovers. When Aristophanes finally gets the floor, he tells the strangest story of the evening, and maybe the easiest one to remember.

First, round people. Long ago, Aristophanes says, humans were round, with four arms, four legs and two faces looking opposite ways. When they ran, they rolled along like tumblers turning cartwheels. There were three kinds: male, female, and a kind that was both. Second, cut in two. They grew so strong and bold that they tried to climb up and attack the gods. Zeus didn't wipe them out. He cut each one in half, and Apollo turned their faces around and drew the skin together at the navel, a mark left as a reminder. Third, the search. Ever since, each half longs for its other half. When two find each other, Aristophanes says, they don't want to be apart even for a moment, though neither can say exactly what they want. Love is the name for that desire and pursuit of the whole. Fourth, a comedy, and an answer. It's a playwright's story, told with a wink, and Plato doesn't give it the last word. Later that night, in the speech we heard yesterday, Diotima says love isn't of a half or a whole unless it is good. Still, the picture has lasted. Some readers hear in it something they know: meeting a person and recognizing them.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who completes something in you: a partner, a friend, a sister or brother, a teacher, someone who supplies what you lack. It doesn't have to be romance. Breathe in and let their face come. Breathe out and notice one thing they bring that you don't. Stay with that for a while, without needing to explain it. After the sit, if you'd like, send them a short thank you, a sentence or two, nothing grand. The bell holds the time.
The other half. Aristophanes' myth in the Symposium: people cut in two, each half searching for the other, and love as the pursuit of the whole. Today's word.
Your line: the half. Today, thank the person who came to mind, and tell them one thing they bring that you don't. Day eight hundred twenty-one.

822.title: Three friendships
822.hook: Aristotle: friendships of use, of pleasure, and of goodness (Nicomachean Ethics 8.3)
822.howItsDone: Aristotle's three kinds of friendship, from books eight and nine of the Nicomachean Ethics, are studied in philosophy and ethics courses, and some readers use them to reflect on their own friendships.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aristophanes and the round people. Your line was the half. Did you thank someone who completes you? Today, from the dinner party to a lecture room, and a word from earlier this week: philia. Day eight hundred twenty-two.

A crowded group chat. Some people are in it because you work together. Some are in it because you have fun together. And maybe one or two are in it because, if everything else fell away, you'd still want them in your life. Aristotle noticed the same sorting long before phones, in his Nicomachean Ethics, and he gave it a shape. Today, his three kinds of friendship, and the slow one at the end.

First, friends of use. Some friendships rest on what each person gets: a coworker, a neighbor who lends tools. Aristotle doesn't sneer at these. But when the usefulness ends, he says, the friendship tends to end too. Second, friends of pleasure. Some rest on enjoyment: people who are fun, who make you laugh. He notices these among the young, who change what they enjoy, and so make and lose friends quickly. Third, friends of the good. The complete kind, Aristotle says, is between people who are good and alike in goodness, who wish good to each other for the other's own sake. These friendships turn out pleasant and useful too, but that isn't why they exist, and they last as long as the people stay good. Fourth, salt eaten together. Such friendships are rare, he says, and slow. As the old saying goes, people can't know each other until they've eaten salt together. The wish for friendship comes fast; the friendship itself takes time. Philia is Aristotle's word for all three kinds. He doesn't call friends of use fake friends. He calls them a smaller kind, and he keeps the larger kind for people who want each other's good.
screen: `FRIENDS OF USE.` · `FRIENDS OF PLEASURE.` · `FRIENDS OF THE GOOD.` · `SALT EATEN TOGETHER.` · then, large: `PHILIA.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Let a few friends' faces come to mind, without ranking them. Notice gently which friendships rest on use, which on enjoyment, and whether one rests on something more: on wanting each other's good. There's no need to judge any of them. If one name stands out, stay with it. Remember the time it took, the meals and the hard days, the salt eaten together. If no name comes, that's an honest answer too, and a friendship like that can still begin. The bell holds the time.
Philia. The Greek word for the love between friends. Aristotle used it for all three kinds: friends of use, of pleasure, and of the good. Today's word.
Your line: friends of the good. Today, name one friend of the good, to yourself or to them, and do one small thing purely for their sake. Day eight hundred twenty-two.

823.title: Another self
823.hook: Aristotle: a friend is another self (Nicomachean Ethics 9.4)
823.howItsDone: Aristotle's idea of the friend as another self, from book nine of the Nicomachean Ethics, is studied in philosophy courses, and some readers use it to reflect on how they treat friends and themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aristotle's three friendships. Your line was friends of the good. Did you do one small thing for a friend's sake? Today, Aristotle goes a step further, in two Greek words. Day eight hundred twenty-three.

Good news arrives, and some people's thumbs go straight to one particular name. Bad news, the same name. Nobody decided that on purpose; it just grew. In the ninth book of his Ethics, Aristotle looks at that kind of bond and asks an odd question. Where does it come from? His answer starts somewhere unexpected: not with the friend at all, but with how a good person lives with themself.
screen: `ONE NAME FOR GOOD NEWS.` → `AN ODD QUESTION.`

segments.voice: First, the marks of a friend. Aristotle lists what people take friendship to mean: wishing good to someone for their sake, wishing them to exist and to live, spending time with them, choosing the same things, sharing their griefs and their joys. Second, it starts at home. Then he turns the list around. A good person, he says, already relates to themself this way: wants their own good, wants to go on living, is glad of their own company, and isn't at war inside. Third, another self. And so, he says, the good person is to a friend as to themself, for a friend is another self. In Greek that's two words, allos autos. The friend isn't a copy. The friend is someone whose good matters to you the way your own does, whose griefs land on you as if they were yours. Fourth, the warning inside. Aristotle turns then to bad people, and draws them as the opposite: at odds with themselves, running from their own company, full of regret for what they've chosen, with no friendly feeling even toward themselves. Some readers take a hopeful thought from the passage: peace inside and friendship outside may grow from the same root, and tending one may help the other.
screen: `THE MARKS OF A FRIEND.` · `IT STARTS AT HOME.` · `ALLOS AUTOS, ANOTHER SELF.` · `THE WARNING INSIDE.` · then, large: `ANOTHER SELF.`

segments.voice: Bring one friend to mind. Breathe in, and wish them what you'd wish yourself today: rest, a good meal, an easy hour, some good news. Breathe out, and if it isn't too hard, wish yourself the same. Go back and forth for a while, friend and self, self and friend, until the two wishes start to sound alike. If one wish comes easily and the other is hard, just notice which one, without judging it. The bell holds the time.
Another self. Aristotle's phrase, allos autos: a friend is someone whose good matters to you the way your own does. Today's word.
Your line: another self. Today, before you reply to a friend, ask how you'd want to be answered, and answer that way. Day eight hundred twenty-three.

824.title: Because it was he
824.hook: Montaigne on his friend La Boétie: because it was he, because it was I (Essays 1.28)
824.howItsDone: Montaigne's essay Of Friendship, from the first book of his Essays, is read in literature and philosophy courses, and some readers turn to it when they're grieving a friend.

segments.voice: Yesterday, allos autos. Your line was another self. Did you answer a friend the way you'd want to be answered? Today, Aristotle's careful lists meet a friendship that wouldn't fit on any list. Day eight hundred twenty-four.

Two men in France have heard about each other for a while, and each is curious about the other. Then, by chance, they meet at a great feast, in the middle of a crowd. By the end of that first meeting, one of them later wrote, they were so taken with each other that nothing was ever again as close to either of them as the other. The writer was Michel de Montaigne. The friend was Étienne de La Boétie. Montaigne's essay about him is called, simply, Of Friendship.
screen: `A FEAST AND A CROWD.` → `MONTAIGNE AND LA BOÉTIE.`

segments.voice: First, the question he can't answer. Montaigne says that if someone pressed him to say why he loved his friend, he could only answer: because it was he, because it was I. No list of reasons, no virtues counted up. Second, the seam disappears. In this friendship, Montaigne says, the two souls were so mingled that the seam joining them couldn't be found. He sets it apart from what he calls common friendships, where, he says, you walk with the bridle in your hand, with prudence and caution. In a friendship like theirs, he says, everything was held in common, so neither could even be said to give the other anything. Third, cut short. La Boétie died, and the friendship ended far sooner than Montaigne wanted. He writes that the rest of his life, set beside the time he had with his friend, was smoke, a long dark night. Fourth, against the list. Two days ago Aristotle explained friendship by what it rests on, and yesterday by its marks. Montaigne doesn't throw that out. But he insists that a friendship like this can't be fully explained from the outside. You can describe it. You can't give its reasons. The reason is the person, two names and nothing else.
screen: `THE QUESTION HE CAN'T ANSWER.` · `THE SEAM DISAPPEARS.` · `CUT SHORT.` · `AGAINST THE LIST.` · then, large: `BECAUSE IT WAS HE.`

segments.voice: Let your deepest friendship come to mind, whether it's going on now, or faded, or lost to death. Don't explain it. Just let the person be there: their face, their voice, something they used to say. If reasons arrive, let them pass by. Rest in the plain fact of them: because it was them. If no friendship like that comes, let the one you'd hope for sit there instead, without a face yet. The bell holds the time.
Because it was he. Montaigne's answer about his friend La Boétie: no reasons, just the person. Because it was he, because it was I. Today's word.
Your line: because it was he. Today, when you catch yourself listing reasons you love someone, stop at their name. Day eight hundred twenty-four.

825.title: As yourself
825.howItsDone: Jews read Leviticus 19 in the Torah cycle as part of the portion called Kedoshim, and Hillel's answer to the man on one foot is taught in Jewish schools and sermons; Christians know the verse through Jesus' quotation of it in the Gospels.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Montaigne and La Boétie. Your line was because it was he. Did you stop at someone's name? Today, the love block turns to Jewish voices, and to a line from Leviticus. Day eight hundred twenty-five.

Leviticus can look like the hard book: offerings, skin diseases, rules for a plague in the walls of a house. Some readers who set out to read the Bible straight through stall right there. But chapter nineteen, in among rules about harvests and wages and fabrics, holds a line some people know by heart without knowing where it comes from. It sits in the middle of a verse, and the first half of that verse changes how it sounds.

First, the whole verse. The King James text reads: "Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." Notice where it lands: right after revenge and grudges. Here, loving the neighbor starts with putting a grudge down. Second, a chapter of neighbors. Around the verse are very practical laws: leave the corners of your field and the fallen grapes for the poor and the stranger; don't keep a worker's wages overnight; don't put a stumbling block before the blind. In Leviticus, love has hands. Third, the great principle. Jewish tradition records Rabbi Akiva calling this verse a great principle of the Torah. And the Talmud tells of a man who asked Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while he stood on one foot. Hillel answered: what is hateful to you, don't do to your fellow. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Now go and learn. Fourth, as yourself. Jesus quotes the same verse in the Gospels, a Jewish teacher quoting the Torah. And the two words at the end quietly assume something: that people want good things for themselves, and that the neighbor's wants are just as real.

Then choose one neighborly thing you could do today: carry something, return something, say good morning by name. The bell holds the time.

Your line: as yourself. Today, do the one neighborly thing you chose, and if a grudge comes along, set it down first. Day eight hundred twenty-five.

826.title: You were strangers
826.hook: love the stranger, for you were strangers in Egypt (Deuteronomy 10:19)
826.howItsDone: Jewish tradition cites the Torah's command to love the stranger, remembering slavery in Egypt, in teaching about welcoming guests and newcomers, and the memory of Egypt is retold each year at the Passover seder.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Leviticus nineteen. Your line was as yourself. Did you do your neighborly thing? Today, the Torah widens the circle past the neighbor, to the one who just arrived. Day eight hundred twenty-six.

The first week in a new place has its own feel. Nobody tells you which door people actually use, how the bus takes payment, who to ask about the trash. You smile too much, or not enough. The Torah returns to that position more than once, the newcomer's, and asks its readers to remember standing in it. This first week of the love block ends right there, with the stranger.
screen: `A FIRST WEEK SOMEWHERE NEW.` → `THE NEWCOMER'S PLACE.`

segments.voice: First, love the stranger. In Deuteronomy, Moses describes God as the one who loves the stranger, giving him food and clothing, and then says: "Love ye therefore the stranger: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The reason isn't an argument. It's a memory. Second, as thyself, again. Yesterday's chapter, Leviticus nineteen, says it too. The stranger who lives with you shall be as one born among you, "and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The love owed to the neighbor is stretched, on purpose, to the outsider. Third, the heart of a stranger. Exodus puts it plainly: "ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." Empathy, in this text, isn't imagination. It's history carried in the body. Fourth, the week in one line. This week climbed Diotima's ladder, met Aristophanes' halves, sorted Aristotle's friends, found another self, sat with Montaigne's because it was he, and read Leviticus. It began with one beautiful face and one chosen friend, and came round to the neighbor. The stranger widens the circle again: someone not chosen, not yet known, whom the Torah asks its readers to welcome anyway.
screen: `LOVE THE STRANGER.` · `AS THYSELF, AGAIN.` · `THE HEART OF A STRANGER.` · `THE WEEK IN ONE LINE.` · then, large: `YOU WERE STRANGERS.`

segments.voice: Sit and let a newcomer come to mind: someone new at work, in your building, at your table, in your town. Breathe in, and remember a time you were the new one: what you didn't know, who helped, who didn't. Breathe out, and let that memory turn toward them. Then find one thing you wish someone had told you when you were new, the door people actually use, the person to ask, and plan to tell it to them. The bell holds the time.
You were strangers. The Torah's reason for loving the outsider: not a theory, but a memory. Ye know the heart of a stranger. Today's word.
Your line: you were strangers. Today, welcome one newcomer by telling them the one thing you wish someone had told you. Day eight hundred twenty-six.
